reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with sudden, severe, generalised abdominal pain in a patient who may have a history of dyspepsia or NSAID use
Examination shows a rigid, board-like abdomen with generalised tenderness, guarding, and absent bowel sounds from peritonitis
Perforation evolves through phases: initial chemical peritonitis from gastric acid, a deceptive period of apparent improvement, and then bacterial peritonitis with sepsis
An erect chest radiograph often shows free air under the diaphragm, but its absence does not exclude perforation; CT is more sensitive
Key risk factors are Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID and aspirin use, smoking, and physiological stress
Initial management is aggressive resuscitation, analgesia, nasogastric decompression, intravenous proton pump inhibition, and broad-spectrum antibiotics while preparing for surgery
The standard operation is closure of the perforation, commonly with an omental (Graham) patch, and thorough peritoneal lavage; large or malignant gastric perforations may require resection
Selected patients with a sealed perforation and no generalised peritonitis may be managed non-operatively with close monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Perforation occurs when a peptic ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the gastric or duodenal wall, allowing gastric and duodenal contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity. Mucosal breakdown is driven by an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs) and mucosal defence. Escaped acidic contents first cause a sterile chemical peritonitis, followed within hours by bacterial contamination and generalised bacterial peritonitis. The resulting inflammatory cascade produces fluid sequestration, sepsis, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure. Duodenal and pyloric ulcers most often perforate anteriorly.
additionalDifferentials: Perforation elsewhere in the GI tract (colonic, appendiceal)
Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy or ovarian pathology
additionalInvestigations: Erect chest radiograph to look for free subdiaphragmatic gas
CT abdomen and pelvis as the most sensitive test for free air and to localise the perforation
Bloods including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, amylase or lipase, CRP, and lactate
Arterial blood gas and group and save or crossmatch for resuscitation and theatre
Helicobacter pylori testing and, later, endoscopy to confirm ulcer healing and exclude malignancy in gastric ulcers
redFlags: Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen and generalised peritonitis (surgical emergency)
Sepsis, haemodynamic instability, or rising lactate indicating septic shock
Deterioration after a deceptive symptom-free interval signalling established bacterial peritonitis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on age, comorbidity, size of perforation, and, critically, the delay before surgery; early intervention gives good recovery, whereas delayed presentation with established peritonitis and sepsis carries high morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding perforation on the basis of a normal erect chest radiograph alone
Being reassured by the transient improvement of the deceptive second phase
Delaying resuscitation and surgery in a septic patient
Failing to biopsy or follow up a perforated gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Resuscitate aggressively with intravenous fluids, analgesia and nasogastric decompression
Commence intravenous proton pump inhibition and broad-spectrum antibiotics covering enteric organisms
Proceed to emergency surgery for operative repair, typically omental (Graham) patch closure of the perforation with peritoneal lavage
Consider non-operative management only in selected, stable, sealed perforations with close monitoring
Test for and eradicate Helicobacter pylori and withdraw NSAIDs to prevent recurrence
Provide postoperative critical-care support for sepsis and organ dysfunction
Arrange follow-up endoscopy to confirm healing and exclude malignancy in gastric ulcers
